title: Data Types & Operators: Strict Equality & Coercion
description: Master JavaScript's primitive types (string, number, boolean, null, undefined) and operators: arithmetic, comparison, and the critical distinction between strict equality (===) and loose equality (==).

objectives.statement: Identify primitive data types (string, number, boolean, null, undefined) and apply strict comparison operators without coercion surprises.
Predict and control type coercion when performing arithmetic and concatenation operations.

content.title: Types and Operators in JavaScript
content.hook: What happens when you add '5' + 5 in JavaScript? You get '55', not 10! Understanding data types and operator behavior is vital to preventing subtle bugs.
content.context: JavaScript values belong to specific types. Primitives include string, number, boolean, null, and undefined. When working with values, strict equality (===) prevents unexpected type conversion.
goals: Understand the 5 primary primitive data types.
Master why triple equals (===) is always preferred over double equals (==).

content.title: Strict Equality vs Loose Equality
content.description: === checks BOTH value and type without conversion (5 === '5' evaluates to false). == performs implicit type coercion (5 == '5' evaluates to true), which often causes unpredictable bugs.

content.prompt: What value will be printed to the console when this script runs?
content.explanation: isStrictMatch is true because 20 === 20. Number('5') explicitly converts '5' to 5, so 20 + 5 = 25. The plus with '-' concatenates to 'true-25'.

feedback.correct: Excellent! Number('5') converts the string to a numeric 5 before addition.
feedback.incorrect: Evaluate each expression step-by-step: 20 === 20 is true; Number('5') is 5; 20 + 5 = 25.

content.title: Build a Price Calculator with Explicit Type Conversion
content.prompt: Given `price = 50` and `discountString = '10'`, convert `discountString` to a number and calculate `finalPrice = price - Number(discountString)`. Then set `const isEligible = finalPrice > 0 && typeof finalPrice === 'number';`.
hints: Use Number(discountString) to convert the string to a number.
Set const isEligible = finalPrice > 0 && typeof finalPrice === 'number';

feedback.correct: Great work! Explicitly converting strings to numbers prevents unwanted concatenation.
feedback.incorrect: Check that you used Number(discountString) and verified typeof finalPrice === 'number'.

content.question: What is the result of `'0' === 0` in JavaScript?

options.text: false, because '0' is a String and 0 is a Number.
true, because both represent the value zero.

content.explanation: Strict equality (===) compares both value and type without coercion. String and number are different types, so the result is false.

feedback.correct: Correct! Strict equality (===) does not coerce types; string and number are different types.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that strict equality requires identical types.

content.title: Data Types & Operators Mastered
takeaways: JavaScript primitive types: string, number, boolean, null, and undefined.
Always use strict equality === and strict inequality !== to avoid type coercion bugs.
Explicitly convert types using Number(), String(), or Boolean() when processing external input.
